metadata.title: 1976 Case 49
metadata.original_presentation: A 64-year-old man was admitted to the hospital because of hematemesis.

required.content: What is the patient's medical history?
required.response: There was a 30-year history of hypertension treated with diuretics. Ten years before admission inferior myocardial infarction occurred, followed by anterior myocardial infarction three years later. Three years before admission congestive heart failure developed, with atrial fibrillation. Cardioversion restored a normal rhythm but was followed by embolic occlusion of the left femoral artery, which required an embolectomy. Digoxin and warfarin were begun. Thirteen months before entry the patient remained in normal rhythm; the warfarin was discontinued when he underwent a urethroplasty because of a urethral injury sustained in a motor-vehicle accident. Seven months before admission atrial fibrillation recurred and persisted. Examination disclosed evidence of an organic brain syndrome, and a CT-scan revealed diffuse cortical atrophy consistent with Alzheimer's disease. Three months before entry he returned to the hospital because of aphasia with mild right hemiparesis and hemihypesthesia. An electrocardiogram again disclosed atrial fibrillation. An echocardiogram showed normal mitral-valve function without evidence of a thrombus, and repeated blood cultures yielded no bacterial growth. Warfarin was resumed, and the patient was discharged home to continue anticoagulant treatment under the regulation of his family.

teaching_points.content: A history of myocardial infarction and atrial fibrillation increases the risk of thromboembolic events.

required.content: What symptoms did the patient experience before admission?
required.response: Three days before admission he came to the Urology Clinic for a urethral dilatation, after which he voided spontaneously, with a good stream. That evening periumbilical crampy pain occurred and radiated in belt-like fashion around the abdomen. He obtained some relief after the ingestion of whisky. Two days before entry he came to the Emergency Ward because of persistent pain. Crampy pain continued, increasing in severity. He passed flatus but no stool. On the evening before admission he became nauseated and vomited coffee-grounds material on several occasions.

teaching_points.content: Coffee-ground emesis suggests upper gastrointestinal bleeding.

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Peptic Ulcer Disease with Bleeding
supporting_evidence: crampy abdominal pain relieved by whisky
refuting_evidence: no direct evidence of ulcer noted yet
additional_information_needed: endoscopy to visualize the gastrointestinal tract

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Gastritis
refuting_evidence: no direct evidence of gastritis noted yet

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Mallory-Weiss Tear
refuting_evidence: no history of retching or forceful vomiting prior to hematemesis
additional_information_needed: endoscopy to identify tear in the esophagus or stomach

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Anticoagulation-related Gastrointestinal Bleeding
refuting_evidence: no INR or coagulation profile provided to assess current anticoagulation status

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Acute Mesenteric Ischemia
key_features: abdominal pain out of proportion to physical findings
refuting_evidence: presence of hematemesis is not typical
no evidence of bowel ischemia or infarction

required.content: What were the findings on physical examination?
required.response: The temperature was 37.2°C, the pulse 100, and the respirations 18. The blood pressure was 130/90 mm Hg. The patient was tremulous, complaining of abdominal pain. The jugular venous pressure was 8 cm of water. The lungs were clear except for a few fine rales at both bases. The heart was enlarged 2 cm beyond the mid-clavicular line, with a +++ left ventricular heave; S2 was normally split; no murmur or S3 sound was heard. The abdomen was slightly distended; the bowel sounds were hypoactive and not high pitched. Tenderness and rebound tenderness were elicited in the mid-portion of the abdomen, without guarding. Rectal examination was negative. The extremities were normal, and neurologic examination was negative except for a right Babinski sign.

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Peptic Ulcer Disease with Bleeding
key_features: history of NSAID or alcohol use
supporting_evidence: abdominal pain relieved by whisky ingestion
refuting_evidence: no specific history of NSAID use or known peptic ulcer disease
additional_information_needed: endoscopy to confirm presence of ulcer

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Gastrointestinal Bleeding due to Anticoagulation
refuting_evidence: no overt signs of over-anticoagulation or INR levels provided
additional_information_needed: history of recent changes in warfarin dosage

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Mesenteric Ischemia
key_features: abdominal pain out of proportion to physical findings
refuting_evidence: absence of severe pain out of proportion to examination
no evidence of bowel ischemia on examination

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Acute Pancreatitis
key_features: abdominal pain radiating to the back
supporting_evidence: abdominal pain radiating in belt-like fashion
refuting_evidence: no history of significant alcohol use
no elevated lipase or amylase levels provided

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Bowel Obstruction
refuting_evidence: hypoactive bowel sounds rather than high-pitched
no guarding or rigidity
additional_information_needed: history of previous surgeries or bowel obstructions

required.content: What were the laboratory test results?
required.response: The urine gave a ++ test for protein; the sediment contained 15 white cells, innumerable red cells and + bacteria per high-power field. The hematocrit was 41.5 per cent; the white-cell count was 12,900, with 91 per cent neutrophils. The prothrombin time was in excess of 30 seconds, with a control of 11 seconds; the partial thromboplastin time was more than 80 seconds. The urea nitrogen was 18 mg, the glucose 175 mg, the bilirubin 0.5 mg, the calcium 10.5 mg, the phosphorus 2 mg, and the protein 10 g (the albumin 5.2 g, and the globulin 4.8 g) per 100 ml. The SGOT was 24 U, the LDH 186 U, the amylase 15 U, and the alkaline phosphatase 4.5 Bodansky U.

teaching_points.content: Prolonged prothrombin time indicates a risk of bleeding.

required.content: What imaging studies were performed and what were the findings?
required.response: An electrocardiogram demonstrated atrial fibrillation at a rate of 130 and changes consistent with old inferior and anterior myocardial infarction. An x-ray film of the chest showed cardiac enlargement with predominance of the left ventricle and a tortuous aorta; the pulmonary vasculature appeared normal, and there was no pleural effusion; the right hemidiaphragm was slightly elevated; the films revealed no change from earlier studies. Films of the abdomen, made with the patient supine and upright, disclosed no evidence of free air; dilated loops of small bowel with air-fluid levels were observed in the left upper quadrant, and there were fluid-filled loops of small bowel, without gas, scattered throughout the remainder of the abdomen. A cystographic study, performed through an indwelling bladder catheter, revealed no evidence of leakage of contrast material.

teaching_points.content: Dilated loops of bowel with air-fluid levels suggest bowel obstruction.

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Upper gastrointestinal bleeding due to peptic ulcer disease
refuting_evidence: no direct evidence of peptic ulcer on imaging
additional_information_needed: endoscopy to visualize the upper GI tract for ulcers or bleeding sources

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Anticoagulation-related gastrointestinal bleeding
refuting_evidence: no direct evidence of bleeding source identified
additional_information_needed: review of INR levels, endoscopy to identify bleeding source

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Small bowel obstruction
key_features: dilated loops of bowel on imaging
supporting_evidence: dilated loops of small bowel with air-fluid levels
refuting_evidence: patient passed flatus
no high-pitched bowel sounds
additional_information_needed: CT scan of the abdomen to confirm obstruction and identify cause

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Mesenteric ischemia
refuting_evidence: no evidence of bowel necrosis or free air on imaging
additional_information_needed: CT angiography to assess mesenteric blood flow

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Acute pancreatitis
refuting_evidence: normal amylase and lipase levels
no evidence of pancreatic inflammation on imaging
additional_information_needed: repeat amylase and lipase levels, abdominal ultrasound or CT scan

required.response: Digoxin and furosemide were given, together with nasogastric suction and fluids and two transfusions of fresh-frozen plasma administered intravenously. On a repeated determination the prothrombin time was 14.9 seconds, with a control of 11 seconds; the partial thromboplastin time was 38.6 seconds.

teaching_points.content: Fresh-frozen plasma can be used to correct coagulopathy.
